archetype.name: Pretender (special-teams driven)
archetype.definition: Winnipeg's 4-1-1 start rests on a red-hot power play, a near-perfect penalty kill, sound goaltending and close-game bounces, while the 5-on-5 play underneath has been below average.

report.headline: First in the Central on bounces and special teams, not even-strength play
report.take:
Winnipeg sits atop the Central at 4-1-1, seventh on the site's Teams tab, a year after a 35-35-12 season that ranked 26th. That is a welcome change, but the record oversells the team. Through six games the Jets have scored 18 and allowed 17, a differential of +1. Their Pts vs Goal Diff of 2.1 is the highest in the league. Every win except the 5-2 game against Minnesota came by a 3-2 score, and the two losses were a one-goal defeat to Boston and a 5-1 loss at home to Anaheim.

The game-to-game engine is special teams and a small group of players. The power play is converting 31.3% of its chances (4th) and the penalty kill is at 92.3% (3rd), so Winnipeg is winning the minutes that are not played at 5-on-5. Kyle Connor has 7 goals on 30 shots and ranks 3rd on the left-wing tab. Cole Perfetti has 5 goals, 5 of his points have come on the power play, and he is 5th among centers. Stuart Skinner has saved 3.3 goals above expected across his four starts. Beyond those three, the scoring thins out quickly. Gabriel Vilardi, Morgan Barron, Viggo Björck and Isak Rosén have no goals between them, which explains why a forward group with a top-five winger and a top-five center grades only D+.

The numbers that usually predict what comes next are the troubling ones. Winnipeg has 45.1% of the 5-on-5 expected goals (26th) and 47% of the shot attempts (23rd), so it is being out-chanced at even strength most nights. The defensive pairs led by Neal Pionk and Mario Ferraro sit in the low 40s in xGF %. The blueline's B grade reflects the rankings of its individual players more than how the team has controlled play. The PDO of 100.6 does not show a team riding unsustainable 5-on-5 percentages. The cushion comes from the power play, the penalty kill and the close-game results, and power plays near 31% and kills above 92% usually come back toward the league average.

This is not a return to the 2024-25 team that ranked 1st with a 52.9% expected-goals share. It looks closer to last year's even-strength profile, with better special teams and a good start in net. Six games is a small sample, and the shot share could improve. For now, the honest read is a bubble-calibre team that has banked some valuable early points.

strengths.title: Elite special teams on both sides
strengths.body: Winnipeg has a top-four power play and a top-three penalty kill, and that has turned even-strength deficits into wins. Connor and Perfetti are driving the power play. Both units are running well above normal league levels, so some cooling should be expected. The 2024-25 team did sustain a 28.9% power play, though, so a strong unit is believable here.

strengths.title: Connor and Perfetti carry the scoring
strengths.body: Connor's 7 goals come on a heavy shot volume, and he ranks 3rd among left wingers. That kind of output tends to hold up better than finishing luck. Perfetti is a top-five center on the site's tab with 8 points. Together they keep the offense near league average despite a thin supporting cast.

strengths.title: Skinner steadying the crease
strengths.body: Skinner has saved goals above expected in his four starts, and the goaltending group grades B+. That matters for a team allowing more chances than it creates. Clay Stevenson's two starts came in below expected, so the starter's form is doing the work.

concerns.title: Losing the 5-on-5 chance battle
concerns.body: Winnipeg's shares of expected goals and shot attempts both sit in the bottom third of the league. The team is spending more time defending than attacking at even strength, and these numbers tend to predict future goal differential better than early win totals do. Unless they improve, the margin for error depends entirely on special teams and goaltending.

concerns.title: Record far ahead of the margin
concerns.body: Nine standings points have come with a +1 goal differential. No team in the league has gotten more points beyond what its goals imply. One-goal wins and overtime results swing back and forth over a season, so the standings position will likely slip unless the underlying play improves.

concerns.title: No scoring depth behind the top two
concerns.body: The forward group grades D+ even with Connor and Perfetti producing. Vilardi has three assists and no goals in 16-plus minutes a night. Barron, Björck and Rosén have one point combined. If the top power-play unit cools, there is little secondary scoring to make up for it.

trend.note: After an opening loss to Boston, Winnipeg won three straight one-goal games, was beaten 5-1 by Anaheim, and then handled Minnesota 5-2. The results have swung more than the steady record suggests.

weekAhead.headline: A soft opener, then the league's best and a sharp Blues team
weekAhead.body:
The week opens in Chicago, the 30th-ranked team on the site. The Blackhawks are getting crushed at 5-on-5, have a leaky penalty kill and get poor goaltending, so this is the game Winnipeg should win and the one where the power play can pad its numbers. Then the Jets come home to face Carolina, ranked 1st, with one of the league's best shot and chance shares, A+ grades at forward and on defense, and the 2nd-best penalty kill. That is a direct test of whether Winnipeg can survive at even strength when its special-teams edge is neutralized.

The week closes in St. Louis. The Blues have 55.1% of the expected goals, which should push play into Winnipeg's end again, but their power play ranks 25th and centers have produced well above expectation against them. Winnipeg's elite penalty kill and its scoring centers, Perfetti and Scheifele, line up well there. A two-win week is the realistic target, and anything less would start to close the gap between the record and the underlying play.

keyMatchups.title: Jets power play vs Chicago's kill
keyMatchups.body: Chicago kills only 75% of its penalties, 24th in the league, and its defense lets every position outscore its expected points. Winnipeg's 4th-ranked power play should feast here. This is the best spot of the week for Connor and Perfetti to keep stacking points.

keyMatchups.title: Even strength against Carolina
keyMatchups.body: Carolina controls nearly 60% of the 5-on-5 expected goals and kills penalties at 93.3%. Winnipeg is unlikely to win this one on special teams. It is the cleanest test of the even-strength weakness, and Skinner may need to steal it.

keyMatchups.title: Winnipeg centers vs St. Louis
keyMatchups.body: St. Louis has let centers score well above their expected points, 28th in the league, and centers account for an outsized share of the points it allows. Perfetti and Scheifele are Winnipeg's best centers. The Blues' 25th-ranked power play also limits what they can do against Winnipeg's kill.

weekAhead.watch: Winnipeg's shot and chance share against Carolina's A+ forwards, the truest read yet on whether this start is real.

restOfSeason.body:
Expect the record to drift toward the play. A team out-chanced at 5-on-5 and leading the league in points beyond its goal differential usually gives back some ground. The power play and penalty kill should stay good but cool from their current pace, and the close-game results will even out. What should hold up is Connor's shot-driven scoring, Perfetti's production and a goaltending group that looks better than last year's. Those keep the Jets in the playoff race rather than back near the bottom of the standings.

The upside case requires the 5-on-5 numbers to climb back toward the near-even shares Winnipeg posted in its strong recent seasons, and the depth centers to start scoring. Without that, this projects as a bubble team leaning on its top line and its goalie, with last year's 35-35-12 still visible underneath the hot start.
swingFactors: Whether the 5-on-5 shot share recovers from the bottom third
Secondary scoring from Vilardi and the depth centers

confidence.note: Six games, with the record leaning heavily on close results and special-teams rates that rarely last.
